# The Tale of the Twin Rivers

In the beginning, two rivers flowed from the same mountain spring—the River of Giving and the River of Keeping. Each was ruled by a spirit: Daleth, who governed Giving, and Keseph, who governed Keeping.

One terrible drought came upon the land. Daleth's river began to dry, her waters nearly gone. Keseph's river, though diminished, still flowed with reserves he had carefully hoarded.

Daleth appeared before Keseph and said, "Brother, share your waters with me, that I might survive. When the rains return, my river will flow abundantly, and I shall return threefold what you give."

Keseph faced an agonizing choice. If he shared, he risked losing everything should the rains never come. If he refused, Daleth would surely perish, and he would remain alone.

After long contemplation, Keseph released half his waters to Daleth's river. The gift sustained her through the drought's darkest days.

When the rains finally returned, Daleth's river swelled magnificently, fed by the widest watershed. True to her word, she sent cascading torrents back to Keseph—far more than threefold.

From that day forth, the rivers intertwined, each strengthening the other, teaching that trust shared in hardship creates abundance for all.

In ancient times, a Wanderer arrived at a great river, desperate to cross but possessing no boat. The River Keeper appeared, offering passage.

"I have only these five silver coins," said the Wanderer. "My life's savings."

The River Keeper smiled. "Give me what you will. Whatever you entrust to me, the river spirits will triple. From that bounty, I shall return what seems fair, and we both shall prosper."

The Wanderer hesitated. To give nothing meant crossing alone, risking the torrents. To give everything meant complete vulnerability.

The Wanderer placed three coins in the River Keeper's palm. The river spirits blessed them, creating nine coins that gleamed in the moonlight.

The River Keeper faced his own choice. He could keep all nine, growing wealthy while the Wanderer remained poor. Or he could honor the implicit covenant between them.

Remembering his own days as a wanderer, the River Keeper returned six coins.

Both prospered that night. The Wanderer crossed safely with enough for his journey. The River Keeper earned his keep and his honor.

From then on, they met each full moon at the river, their mutual trust creating abundance that flowed like water, enriching both shores.
